content: Long waiting times for elective healthcare procedures can lead to significant distress for patients, potentially worsening their health outcomes and reflecting poorly on the organization and planning of healthcare services. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions designed to reduce waiting times for elective diagnostic and therapeutic care. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others. Additional sources such as trial registries, grey literature, and reference lists of relevant articles were also examined. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), controlled before-after studies (CBAs), and interrupted time series (ITS) designs that met EPOC's minimum criteria. The studies assessed interventions targeting waiting times for elective procedures, with outcomes measured as the number or proportion of participants exceeding or meeting specific waiting time thresholds, or the mean/median waiting times. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias for each study using standardized tools. Interventions were categorized into three groups: (1) those aimed at rationing or prioritizing demand, (2) those focused on expanding capacity, and (3) those restructuring the intake assessment or referral process. For RCTs, preand post-intervention outcomes were reported, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. ITS studies were reanalyzed using segmented time-series regression to estimate changes in level and slope. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising three RCTs and five ITS studies. These studies involved 135 general practices/primary care clinics, seven hospitals, and one outpatient clinic. The interventions, procedures, and clinical conditions studied were highly heterogeneous, precluding meta-analysis. One ITS study evaluated a prioritization system for elective surgery services and found that it reduced the number of semi-urgent patients waiting longer than the recommended 90 days by 28 patients per month. However, no significant effects were observed for urgent cases (less than 30 days) or non-urgent cases (less than 365 days). Interventions aimed at restructuring the intake assessment or referral process were examined in seven studies. Four studies (two RCTs and two ITS studies) evaluated open access or direct booking/referral systems. One RCT demonstrated that open access to laparoscopic sterilization reduced waiting times, but the study suffered from very high attrition (87%). Another RCT showed that open access to investigative services reduced waiting times by 30% for patients with lower urinary tract syndrome (LUTS) but had no impact on waiting times for patients with microscopic hematuria. In one ITS study, same-day scheduling for pediatric health clinic appointments directly reduced waiting times by 25.2 days, with an additional monthly reduction of 3.03 days thereafter. However, another ITS study found no effect of a direct booking system on the proportion of patients receiving colposcopy appointments within the recommended timeframe. One RCT and one ITS study evaluated distant consultancy methods, such as instant photography for dermatological conditions and telemedicine for ear, nose, and throat (ENT) conditions, but neither showed any effect on waiting times. Similarly, another ITS study found no impact of a pooled waiting list on the number of patients waiting for uncomplicated spinal surgery. The overall quality of evidence, assessed using the GRADE tool, ranged from low to very low. Notably, no studies were identified that evaluated interventions aimed at increasing capacity or rationing demand. In conclusion, the limited number of low-quality studies available prevents definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of interventions to reduce waiting times for elective procedures. However, interventions that improve service accessibility, such as open access or direct booking/referral systems, show some potential in reducing waiting times. Further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings and explore other strategies.
